resources.headline: GEO Is A Distraction: Here’s Where The Real Opportunity Is via @sejournal, @marie_haynes
resources.fullText: AI is absolutely rewriting how the internet works, but optimizing for large language model visibility misses where the actual return on investment exists as the web morphs from a place to find information to the agentic web. Have you measured how many of your website’s visitors come from LLM tools like ChatGPT? I looked at 12 months of GA4 data across 100 different websites of varying sizes with over 145 million sessions. In this dataset, sessions from ChatGPT amounted to just 0.62% of the volume driven by Google Organic. That’s not a typo. 0.62%. When all other LLMs were included in this number, it increased to 0.73%. I asked Gemini 4 Argon in Antigravity to turn this into a graphic to help me visualize the scale of this: Image Credit: Marie Haynes While it’s interesting to measure and try to influence whether your content is being cited by ChatGPT, for the vast majority of sites this traffic is miniscule compared to Google organic visitors! What About Conversions? Of the 100 sites in my dataset, 55 were tracking conversions in GA4. I did indeed find that ChatGPT visitors converted at a higher rate. Google organic visitors converted at a rate of 3.02%. ChatGPT visitors converted at a rate of 13.8%. However, even though ChatGPT visitors converted at more than 4.5x the rate of Google organic visitors, Google still drove 96.5% of the total conversions across all channels analyzed. In my small dataset, Google organic drove 27x more conversions than all LLMs combined. Image Credit: Marie Haynes Will this change as LLM adoption grows? When ChatGPT had been out for a few months, many of us looked at the clicks from ChatGPT, saw they were increasing, and predicted that if the exponential trend continued, LLMs would eventually send far more traffic than Google. We were wrong. I tasked Antigravity with looking at those 100 properties and calculating the collective total of visits from ChatGPT. In August of 2025, in conjunction with the release of GPT-5, the exponential growth of ChatGPT sessions ended. In fact, ChatGPT has been sending fewer and fewer visitors to websites since then. Image Credit: Marie Haynes Yes, AI Is Changing Search, But Google Is Still The Most Important Search Engine There’s so much focus in our industry on “GEO” – optimizing for generative engines. It boggles my mind how much money has been raised and earned by companies that track your mentions in ChatGPT and other LLM tools. We are chasing the new thing! We can all see that AI is changing how businesses are found on the internet, but I think we’re missing the point by putting so much emphasis on people finding us via ChatGPT and similar LLMs. The AI search that is actually sending people to businesses today isn’t ChatGPT. It’s Google. Between AI Overviews, AI Mode, and a core ranking system that is now largely driven by AI, millions of people are using AI search every day without ever leaving Google. We can lament over the fact that our clicks to informational content are drying up, but the reality is that the web is changing. If people are looking to engage with a business like yours, then Google Search is by far the most likely way they will find you. The problem is, it is difficult for us to measure our progress. Rank tracking means little. Search Console gives us some information but little that’s immediately actionable. I would encourage you to work on figuring out what a conversion or key event looks like for your business and tracking it. Surprisingly, 45 out of the 100 sites I randomly sampled were not tracking any key events! Then work towards improving those metrics. Focus on improving user satisfaction far more than optimizing for machines. Today’s Google’s ranking systems are heavily influenced by deep learning (AI) algorithms that are continually working to predict what it is a searcher will find the most helpful. I’d love to see more of my amazing colleagues (aka you perhaps?) publish information to show how you are shifting your efforts in this new and unfamiliar era of Search. Here’s one from Wil Reynolds. If you can figure out how to track and measure your progress as Search changes, you have valuable insights that will help others in our industry! Start Thinking About The Opportunities In Agentic Search Google’s CEO Sundar Pichai recently said that “Search will become an agent manager.” This means that Search shifts from being a passive way to find links to an active work coordinator. I don’t think anyone, even people from inside Google, can predict how the next era of search will unfold. At Google I/O last year, I filmed this clip where Sergey Brin was asked what the web will look like in 10 years. He said it was impossible to predict. “I don’t think we really know what the world looks like in 10 years.” Then Demis Hassabis said: “The web is going to change quite a lot if you think about an agent-first web, like it doesn’t necessarily need to see renders and things like we do as humans using the web. So I think things will be pretty different in a few years.“ I don’t know what the web will look like in 10 years, but we have a good idea of the types of things that are going to change it in the next few years. Google’s Universal Cart The Universal Cart aggregates products from multiple retailers into a unified checkout within Google Wallet. It actively monitors price adjustments, promotions, and restocks. Searchers are able to add products from multiple vendors and then check out without ever visiting their sites. Where the opportunity lies: Get to really know Google’s Merchant Center. There is a new AI assistant in Merchant Center that I find quite helpful. If you can master Merchant Center data, you’ll perhaps be able to see more of your products bundled into Universal Carts. Universal Commerce Protocol Governed by Google, Shopify, and Stripe, UCP provides the open discovery layer for AI agents to compare inventory and purchase natively, keeping your client as Merchant of record. People will be able to
keyNotes: Even though everyone talks about AI tools like ChatGPT, the article found that traffic from them to websites is incredibly small – only about 0.73% compared to what Google sends.
While people who *do* come from ChatGPT are much more likely to buy something (they convert 4.5 times more often), Google still brings in almost all the actual sales, driving 96.5% of all purchases.
Contrary to early predictions, the number of visitors coming from ChatGPT has actually been *decreasing* since August 2025, showing that its initial rapid growth didn't continue.
The real AI search happening today is *within Google*, which uses AI for its search results and features, meaning people are already using AI to find businesses without ever leaving Google.
Many businesses are missing out by not tracking what actually leads to sales or important actions on their websites; the article found 45 out of 100 sites weren't tracking these key events.
resources.question: The article suggests that Google is becoming an "agent manager," meaning it might coordinate purchases directly for people, sometimes without them even visiting your website, like with the "Universal Cart." If this is the future, how might you need to rethink how your business attracts customers and completes sales?

resources.headline: How to identify content gaps for AI visibility
resources.fullText: Learning how to identify content gaps for AI visibility starts with a question that traditional content gap analysis doesn’t always answer: where could a brand contribute something useful to an AI-generated answer, but isn’t being mentioned or cited? With AI and SEO trends changing how people discover brands, finding a content gap isn’t always as simple as identifying a missing article. A company might already have a relevant page that AI search engines aren’t citing, or an AI assistant might mention the brand while relying on another website for supporting information. Creating more content without understanding what’s missing may not solve the problem. This guide walks through how to use prompt-tracking data and existing content to identify AI visibility gaps, review competing sources, and decide what to do next. Table of Contents What is an AI visibility content gap and how is it different from SEO gaps? How to Identify Content Gaps for AI Visibility Step-by-Step How to Analyze AI and Search Results to Understand What to Fix How to Create or Update Content to Close AI Visibility Gaps How to Measure Results and Iterate Common Pitfalls to Avoid When You Identify Content Gaps for AI Visibility Tools and Templates to Speed Up Content Gap Analysis Frequently Asked Questions About Identifying Content Gaps for AI Visibility Close the gaps that matter, not every gap that appears. What is an AI visibility content gap, and how is it different from SEO gaps? An AI visibility content gap is a relevant information need, represented by a prompt or group of prompts, for which a brand is absent from AI-generated answers, lacks supporting citations, or does not have content that adequately addresses the question. Traditional content gap analysis typically compares a website’s keyword coverage and search performance with competing websites. It helps marketers identify topics and queries that competitors rank for, but their own websites do not. AI SEO uses artificial intelligence to support traditional SEO tasks, such as keyword research, content analysis, and optimization. Both approaches — traditional SEO and AI-assisted SEO — focus on improving a website’s performance in traditional search results. AI visibility analysis examines a different set of outcomes. A page can rank well in Google and still be absent from a ChatGPT, Gemini, or Perplexity response. And, to add to the complexity, an AI assistant may mention a brand without directing readers to the brand’s website at all. That difference makes it important to understand three types of AI visibility gaps: Free AEO Guide: HubSpot's Guide to AI Engine Optimization Navigate the AI revolution with proven strategies to optimize your content for AI visibility. How answer engines rank and choose content Practical templates and checklists AEO strategies that convert 27% of AI traffic to leads Real examples from HubSpot's AEO implementation Download for Free Learn more Download for Free Download FreeAll fields are required. Form not available You're all set! Click this link to access this resource at any time. Download Now What it means Example Potential action Coverage gap The brand lacks a page that adequately answers a relevant question. AI visibility consultancy has a services page but no resource explaining when a company should choose a consultant-led audit instead of a monitoring platform. Create a page or expand an existing resource to address the unmet need. Extractability gap A relevant page exists, but its useful information is difficult to locate, interpret, or reuse. A detailed feature page describes capacity planning in promotional language without clearly explaining the workflow. Improve the explanation, headings, examples, and presentation of key facts. Citation-support gap The brand appears in an answer, or has relevant content, but another source provides the evidence used to support the response. An AI assistant recommends the platform but cites a third-party comparison for its capabilities. Review the cited evidence and strengthen the brand’s supporting documentation where appropriate. View all rows View fewer rows For marketers, treat these categories as diagnostic rather than mutually exclusive. A page may cover the right topic but lack both a direct answer and sufficient evidence to support a citation. The objective is to identify what is missing from the answer ecosystem, not simply what is missing from a content calendar. AI Mentions vs. AI Citations An AI mention occurs when an answer names a brand, product, or company. An AI citation occurs when the answer provides a source reference or link supporting information in the response. For marketers, understanding these differences in outcomes makes it easier to identify content opportunities. For example, an AI assistant answering “What are the best project management tools for agencies?” might recommend a particular platform but cite an independent review site for its pricing, integrations, or suitability. The brand has achieved mention visibility, but its own content is not necessarily being used as the supporting source. A citation to the brand’s website provides a different signal. A citation to the brand’s website means the assistant has surfaced that website as a source for the answer. However, a citation alone does not establish that the assistant recommended the brand, that a reader clicked the link, or that the answer generated revenue. Pro tip: Record mentions and citations separately. A brand can be mentioned in an AI answer without citing a single piece of its own content as a source. That is a completely different situation with a completely different fix, and combining them into a single visibility metric can conceal whether the opportunity involves brand inclusion, source selection, or both. How to Identify Content Gaps for AI Visibility Step-by-Step An AI visibility content gap analysis follows four steps: collect relevant prompt data, classify mentions and citations
keyNotes: Surprisingly, even if your website ranks high in Google, an AI assistant like ChatGPT or Gemini might not use your information. This new idea of an "AI visibility gap" means your brand could be missing from AI answers even with great content.

Simply creating more articles won't fix this problem; you need to understand *why* AI isn't using your content. This could be because you lack a page on a topic, your existing page is hard for AI to understand, or AI is citing someone else for details about your brand.

There are three main reasons AI might miss your content: you don't have a page on a topic (a "coverage gap"), your existing page is hard for AI to pull information from (an "extractability gap"), or AI mentions your brand but uses another website as evidence (a "citation-support gap").

It's important to know the difference between an AI assistant just *naming* your brand (a "mention") and actually *linking* to your website as a source of information (a "citation"). A mention is good, but a citation means the AI found your content useful enough to point to it directly.

Instead of trying to fill every possible content gap, the goal is to figure out what's missing from the overall "answer ecosystem" that AI uses, not just what's missing from your company's list of articles.
resources.question: The article explains that an AI assistant might recommend a brand but then cite a different website for supporting details about that brand's capabilities. If you discovered an AI was mentioning your work or product but relying on *someone else's* information to explain it, what specific steps would you take to make sure your own content becomes the trusted source for AI?

resources.headline: Which AI prompts should you track? A practical guide
resources.fullText: For most teams, the answer to “which prompts should I track?” is this: track a representative sample of branded, unbranded, and competitor prompts across buyer stages, personas, and priority markets. Don’t fall into the trap of tracking everything. Remember: buyers don’t query answer engines the way they query Google. A prompt often reads like a brief. Prompts often include details like team size, budget, location, and follow-up questions that all reshape the answer. Faced with that variation, marketers either track everything and drown in noise or fall back on branded queries that inflate visibility metrics. This guide aims to help marketers build an effective prompt tracking set. The guide explains choosing and balancing prompts as well as scoring, maintaining, and turning visibility and citation findings into content decisions. Table of Contents Which prompts should I track to reflect real buyer intent? Which prompts should I track for awareness vs. decision? Which prompts should I track first, and how many should I start with? Which prompts should I track based on CRM-informed business context? Which prompt tracking engines, locations, and cadence should I use? Which prompts should I track to prove business impact? Which prompts should I track for ongoing reporting and page-level fixes? How to Tell Which Prompts Are Working How do I maintain my prompt set quarterly? How to Configure Prompt Tracking In HubSpot AEO Frequently Asked Questions About Prompt Tracking. Track fewer prompts, but track smarter. Which prompts should I track to reflect real buyer intent? According to Responsive research, 56% of tech buyers are turning to generative AI to build vendor shortlists. Answer engines increasingly drive which brands buyers consider before they ever visit a website. Tracking prompts shows marketers whether their brand appears where buyers are asking, how it’s described, and which competitors and sources are winning those answers instead. HubSpot AEO Tool See exactly where your brand shows up in answer engines and take action to close AI visibility gaps. Track AI mentions. Analyze citations Monitor prompts Benchmark competitors Learn more. How do branded, unbranded, and competitor prompts work? Think about prompts in three broad categories: branded, unbranded, and competitor. Branded Prompts Branded prompts include the company or product name, such as “What is [Brand]?” or “Does [Brand] integrate with Salesforce?” Important note: In the same way that a brand will rank for its branded keyword in traditional SEO, answer engines should always mention the brand here, so presence isn’t the metric. Branded prompts protect brand accuracy in AI answers. For branded prompts, the focus is sentiment and accuracy. Unbranded Prompts Unbranded prompts describe a problem or category without naming any company, such as “best project management software for agencies” or “how to reduce client onboarding time.” Unbranded solution-seeking prompts measure discovery-stage visibility. Unbranded prompts usually reveal the biggest gaps and should make up the largest share of a prompt set. In my experience, unbranded prompts deserve the same priority as unbranded keywords in traditional SEO. Search teams often judge search performance by branded demand, but search teams and stakeholders must understand that nonbranded search plays a critical role in performance as well. Increasing brand visibility is mostly the job of PR, brand marketing, and wider visibility efforts. Search supports that work, but a search team’s core role is to reach buyers who are still discovering their options and don’t yet know which brands to consider. In AI search, unbranded prompts are where that discovery happens. Unbranded prompts are the clearest measure of whether answer engine optimization (AEO) is reaching new buyers, tying visibility as directly as possible to a search team’s efforts. Competitor Prompts Competitor prompts reveal where rivals appear during evaluation. Competitor prompts name one or more rivals, such as “Is [Competitor] good for remote teams?” or “alternatives to [Competitor].” Answers to these prompts show which brands answer engines consider as the category’s default options, and whether the brand appears as a credible alternative. Pro Tip: If possible, track prompts for three to five direct competitors. Keep the focus on competitors who have solid marketing strategies and perform well online. Ideally, marketers will track prompts that fall under all three categories of branded, unbranded, and competitor. Example #1 Example #2 Example #3 Branded What is [Brand]? What does [Brand] do for agencies? [Brand] vs. [Competitor] [Brand] pricing and plans Unbranded How do agencies keep client projects on track? What types of project management software exist? Best project management tools for agencies Most affordable project management tool with time tracking Competitor What is [Competitor] used for? Is [Competitor] good for remote teams? Alternatives to [Competitor] [Competitor] pricing vs. alternatives View all rows View fewer rows Using dedicated tools for prompt tracking, instead of manual checks, makes spotting trends more manageable for marketers. HubSpot’s AEO tool gives marketers one place to monitor prompts and track brand visibility across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity. Teams can compare how often competitors appear on the same prompts, review which sources answer engines cite, and turn findings into clear, prioritized recommendations. For Marketing Hub Professional and Enterprise customers, AEO is included and uses CRM data to suggest prompts to track, rather than relying on generic industry templates. HubSpot’s AEO tool is also available standalone for $50/month (25 prompts included). How should I balance my prompt mix? A balanced prompt mix can look slightly different for different businesses. One thing that stays the same is that a balanced prompt mix puts most tracking effort where visibility is uncertain,
keyNotes: It turns out a lot of tech buyers, specifically 56%, are now using AI tools to find companies they might want to work with, even before they visit a company's website. This means what AI says about a business is becoming a crucial way for people to discover new options.

Instead of trying to keep tabs on every single question people ask AI, it's much more effective to pick a smaller, smart selection of questions. This helps you understand what real customers are asking without getting overwhelmed.

The article breaks down the kinds of questions you should track into three helpful groups: those that mention your company by name, those that ask about a problem or solution without naming anyone, and those that specifically mention your competitors.

The questions that don't mention any specific company (called "unbranded prompts") are usually the most important to watch. They show whether your business is reaching new customers who are just starting to look for solutions, and they should make up the biggest part of your tracking efforts.

By watching these AI questions, you can see if your company is appearing in AI answers, how it's being described, and which other companies are being recommended instead. This information can then help you decide what content to create.

resources.headline: The Salesforce Full-Court Press On Revenue Orchestration Platforms
resources.fullText: < Featured Blogs Home > Featured Blogs > The Salesforce Full-Court Press On Revenue Orchestration Platforms The Salesforce Full-Court Press On Revenue Orchestration Platforms The revenue orchestration platform (ROP) market is entering a new phase as Salesforce increases competitive pressure on established ROP providers. For years, providers such as Gong, Salesloft, Outreach, Aviso, Revenue.io, and others benefited from a simple reality: Salesforce was the system of record, but it was rarely the preferred place to work. Specialist providers created better experiences for prospecting, forecasting, coaching, pipeline inspection, and revenue execution. Today, Salesforce is investing to change that dynamic. The combination of new capabilities along with a series of acquisitions, points to a concerted effort to make revenue orchestration a native Salesforce capability rather than a category adjacent to Salesforce. Recent category evaluations have reflected Salesforce’s increased focus on platform capability. Historically, Salesforce owned customer records while specialist providers owned execution. But as Salesforce expands into intelligence, orchestration, agent management, and seller interaction, that separation is becoming less distinct. The result is a far more direct competitive overlap than many ROP providers have faced previously. The following factors are driving this resurgence: Salesforce’s strategy aligns with emerging buying priorities. Salesforce’s strategy has become both more coherent and more relevant to where the market is heading. Historically, revenue orchestration was viewed as a collection of capabilities: Forecasting Sales engagement Conversation intelligence Pipeline management Coaching Workflow automation But today the market is also beginning to focus on: Shared context Agentic execution Workflow orchestration Cross-functional coordination Governance AI interoperability These are areas where Salesforce naturally has advantages with a vision centered on shared context, agentic execution, interoperable AI, and a unified execution layer spanning workflows, agents, and experiences. Salesforce is finally connecting the dots. For years, Salesforce had many of the underlying components, but they often were disconnected. Salesforce is doing a better job at helping buyers understand how these newer capabilities come together to tell a coherent story about how revenue work might operate in an agent-mediated world: CRM Data 360 Momentum Slackbot Agentforce MCP interoperability Claudeforce SIForce Koa The Forrester Wave™: Revenue Orchestration Platforms For B2B, Q3 2026 specifically recognized Salesforce’s evolution from a traditional system of record into a platform combining CRM data, conversational context, workflows, agents, and AI-assisted revenue execution. Market priorities are shifting. Buyers are evaluating broader operational and tech strategy questions beyond just seller productivity, including: How do I consistently coordinate execution? How do I govern agents? How do I coordinate actions? How do I preserve context? How do I orchestrate work across functions? How do I avoid creating another AI silo? How do I avoid vendor lock-in? Should I build or buy? Salesforce has invested heavily in governance, orchestration, and administration capabilities that address many of these concerns. The Wave evaluation highlighted strengths in governance, administration, data quality, extensibility, and ecosystem reach. Those were not historically the primary buying criteria for revenue orchestration platforms but are now becoming more important. Salesforce has embraced headless architecture. ROP providers have differentiated and grown by exploiting gaps in Salesforce capability and user experience. Sellers might store data in CRM but spend much of their day elsewhere. Historically, Salesforce competed by encouraging users to spend more time inside Salesforce. Claudeforce introduces a different possibility. Salesforce may no longer need to own the user interface if it can own the data, context, permissions, workflows, and actions underneath it. Claudeforce turns Claude into a conversational gateway to Salesforce, while Slackbot extends those same capabilities into everyday collaboration, allowing users to access data, insights, and actions without opening Salesforce itself. The common assumption has been that structured revenue work requires structured applications. Capabilities such as cadence management, forecasting, and coaching are structured activities that required structured interfaces, but Claudeforce challenges a variation of that assumption: not that structured work needs structure but that structured work requires a dedicated application interface. Claudeforce may allow Salesforce to bypass many historical CRM usability challenges altogether. Salesforce no longer needs sellers to love Salesforce. It may only need them to love Claude. If sellers can remain within more flexible and dynamic AI environments while Salesforce quietly handles execution behind the scenes, long-standing objections about CRM complexity become less relevant. Despite Progress, Salesforce Hasn’t “Solved” Revenue Orchestration While the developments discussed above represent real progress and reward a renewed focus on delivering more value and impact for frontline sellers, this should not be interpreted yet as “Salesforce has solved revenue orchestration.” While market analysts appear to support the direction Salesforce is going, important challenges remain to be addressed. These include: Inconsistent user experience. In the Forrester Wave evaluation, Salesforce demonstrated a mature and highly capable user experience but not an entirely consistent or seamless one. The evaluation also found that experience quality remains heavily influenced by implementation and configuration choices. keyNotes: Salesforce, a major company known for managing customer information, is making a big push to become the central hub for how businesses organize all their selling activities, from finding new customers to closing deals. This means they want to offer all the tools needed for this process themselves, rather than relying on other specialized companies.

For a long time, other companies like Gong and Salesloft were better at specific selling tasks, even though Salesforce held the main customer records. Now, Salesforce is investing heavily and buying other companies to offer these specialized tools directly, creating more competition for those smaller players.

Salesforce is changing its approach by connecting its various tools and even using a new method called 'headless architecture.' This means their software can work in the background, allowing people to access Salesforce information and take action through other apps like Claude or Slack, without ever having to open Salesforce directly.

This shift by Salesforce is happening because businesses are now looking for more than just tools for individual salespeople; they want systems that can coordinate entire teams, manage how artificial intelligence (AI) works across different tools, and avoid getting stuck with one vendor. Salesforce is trying to meet these broader needs.

Despite all these new developments, Salesforce hasn't completely perfected how businesses organize their selling efforts. The article points out that their tools still have some issues, like not always providing a perfectly smooth experience for users, which often depends on how they are set up.

resources.headline: The Junior Hiring Gap Your 2027 Marketing Budget Should Name via @sejournal, @gregjarboe
resources.fullText: Treat your 2027 entry-level hires as their own budget line and not part of overall headcount. The best current payroll data shows that employment in AI-exposed jobs is shifting, with fewer junior hires rather than layoffs. Most marketing budget discussions are looking somewhere else. In July, I argued that chief marketing officers should fund five functions instead of legacy channel buckets. In September, I argued that SEO and paid media managers become directors by proving AI pays for itself while keeping their teams intact. Stanford’s Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar, and Ruyu Chen, and Kevin Indig’s October planning memo, support parts of both arguments. They also expose a gap. What Stanford Measured, And What It Can’t Tell You The Stanford Digital Economy Lab working paper, revised Aug. 12, 2026, draws on anonymized ADP payroll records. The analysis sample is a balanced panel of firms with between 3.5 and 5 million employees per month, running through June 2026. The headline finding is that employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed occupations stands 19% below where it would be if it had kept pace with their less-exposed peers. In raw terms, the two most exposed quintiles of young workers fell about 11% since November 2022, while the three least-exposed quintiles grew about 10%. Experienced workers show no comparable gap. Every older age group grew over the same period, by as much as 11% for workers aged 35 to 40. The mechanism matters more than the headline. The authors say the divergence works mainly through reduced hiring of young workers, and separations among young workers fell at least as much in the most exposed occupations as in the least exposed. That is the opposite of what displacement would imply. The declines concentrate where AI substitutes for human tasks. Where AI complements workers, employment is flat or rising, especially for experienced workers, and the adjustment shows up in employment, not in pay. The authors of the Stanford paper call the facts “early, descriptive indicators,” and say the work does not estimate a causal impact of AI. The pattern shrinks when they control for education, from about -0.18 to -0.09 in their primary sample, and the smaller figure is significant only at the 10% level. Earlier versions of the paper reported regression estimates of 13% and 16%, and the headline measure has since changed, so the 19% should not be lined up against those numbers. The paper also measures occupations broadly. It reports no SEO or marketing figures. My July Column Holds Up, With 1 Missing Line In my previous article, 2027 Marketing Budgets, I told CMOs to rebuild the budget around five functions, one of them human judgment and editorial oversight. I also cited Gartner data showing labor rising from a mean 21.9% to 24.5% of marketing budgets, even though 43% of CMOs expected to cut labor spending. Stanford’s paper supports the editorial oversight budget line. Where AI complements workers, employment holds or grows, especially for experienced workers. That describes the editors and strategists I argued CMOs should be able to defend. What the column did not say is who that labor money pays for. My view is that the extra labor share is going to experienced people, while the seats that would have gone to 22- to 25-year-olds in exposed jobs are quietly left empty. Gartner doesn’t split marketing labor by seniority, and Stanford doesn’t break out marketing, so I can’t prove it. But a budget that raises labor share while freezing entry-level hiring has not told the CFO what it is funding, and I think that omission will be the first thing a sharp finance chief finds. See also: How To Restructure Your Marketing Team & Budget For The AI-Search Era My September Column Needs A Sharper Test In my other article about how an SEO or paid manager can become a director, I said the managers most likely to move up are the ones who can prove AI pays for itself while keeping their teams intact. The Stanford paper finds the adjustment happens through hiring and not through layoffs. A team can be fully intact on the day a manager presents the scorecard and still be shrinking, because the junior seat that would have been filled this year never was. “Intact” tells you who is still there. It says nothing about who was NOT hired. If the entry-level pipeline narrows, the pool for the next generation of managers narrows with it. That is my inference, not something the paper tests, and it is the part of this story I would watch most closely. One more reconciliation. The Harvard Business School study I cited in September looked at job postings through March 2025, so it is a demand signal. Stanford measures realized employment through June 2026. They point the same direction, but I would not add the 13% and the 19% together. Kevin Indig Gives The Gap Somewhere To Land Kevin Indig’s Growth Memo on planning 2027, summarized in a LinkedIn post, starts from a premise I share. Salaries, tools, and infrastructure are fixed costs, so the real budget question is which capabilities to fund. Proven work such as technical SEO, content refreshes, and digital PR that earns citations gets full funding, while unmeasurable bets get their own line based on judgment. Screenshot from LinkedIn, October 2026 The memo goes further than the post. It adds a capped bucket for learning work, with one owner and a decision date, and argues that community work needs a named owner and fixed weekly hours or it gets cut first. It suggests roughly 5% of the marketing budget for community, sometimes 10%. His three measurement layers also fill a hole in my September scorecard, which tracked hours saved, hours returned, outcomes, and cost. Kevin says to set targets for “exposure (AI citations, mentions, share of voice), behavior (branded search, direct visits), and business outcomes (pipeline),” and to read them together. If exposure rises while branded search stays flat, he says, you have a distribution problem. Put
keyNotes: Surprisingly, AI isn't causing widespread job losses, but it is quietly reducing opportunities for young people: employment for workers aged 22 to 25 in jobs affected by AI is 19% lower than it would be if it kept pace with less-exposed roles, mainly because companies are hiring fewer of them.
Even though marketing budgets are spending more on people (labor costs rose from 21.9% to 24.5% of budgets), this money seems to be going to experienced staff, leaving entry-level roles empty.

The article suggests that companies should create a specific budget line just for entry-level hires, rather than lumping them into general staff numbers, to make sure these crucial junior positions aren't overlooked.

While it might seem like AI helps experienced workers, the article warns that if junior positions aren't filled, the future pool of experienced managers also shrinks over time, creating a long-term problem for team growth.
resources.question: The article highlights that AI is leading to fewer entry-level hires, even as overall spending on people in marketing goes up. If your industry or company is seeing similar trends, how might you specifically budget or plan to ensure you're still developing the next generation of talent, rather than just relying on experienced staff?
